definition: Gesture recognition is an area of research and development in computer science and language technology concerned with the recognition and interpretation of human gestures.
details: A subdiscipline of computer vision, it employs mathematical algorithms to interpret gestures. Gesture recognition offers a path for computers to begin to better understand and interpret human body language, previously not possible through text or unenhanced graphical user interfaces (GUIs). Gestures can originate from any bodily motion or state, but commonly originate from the face or hand. One area of the field is emotion recognition derived from facial expressions and hand gestures. Users can make simple gestures to control or interact with devices without physically touching them. Many approaches have been made using cameras and computer vision algorithms to interpret sign language, however, the identification and recognition of posture, gait, proxemics, and human behaviors is also the subject of gesture recognition techniques.

explainer.lead: Gesture recognition lets computers interpret human movements, especially those of the face and hands, as meaningful gestures. It can turn body language into a way to control devices without touching them and can help computers interpret expressions and behavior.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a friend who understands when you wave or give a thumbs-up without you saying anything. Gesture recognition teaches a computer to do something similar by watching movements and working out what they mean. That movement can then become an instruction for a device.
tiers.practitioner: Gesture recognition is applied with cameras, computer vision methods, and mathematical algorithms to interpret gestures for device interaction. Implementations may target facial expressions, hand gestures, sign language, posture, gait, proxemics, or other human behavior, so the intended gesture set must be clear. A common pitfall is treating the field as only touchless hand control when it also includes recognition of broader bodily states and behavior.
tiers.paperLevel: Gesture recognition is the computer-science and language-technology problem of mapping human bodily motion or state to an interpreted gesture, commonly through computer vision and mathematical algorithms. In plain notation, the task can be viewed as G = f(O), where O is an observation of bodily motion or state and G is its recognized interpretation. Its scope includes facial expressions, hand gestures, sign language, posture, gait, proxemics, and human behaviors rather than a single input modality or task.

explainer.example: A user makes a simple hand gesture in front of a camera. Computer vision algorithms recognize the movement as a predefined gesture, and the device responds to it without the user touching a screen or control.

explainer.intuition: People communicate through movements and bodily states as well as words. Gesture recognition gives a computer a way to observe those cues and interpret them as gestures, expanding interaction beyond text and unenhanced graphical user interfaces.
howItWorks: A gesture originates from bodily motion or state, commonly involving the face or hand.
A camera captures the person's movement or expression.
Computer vision and mathematical algorithms interpret the observed gesture.
The recognized meaning can support device control or further interpretation, such as emotion recognition.
explainer.whyItMatters: It provides a route for computers to interpret aspects of human body language that text and unenhanced GUIs do not capture. This supports touchless interaction and research into expressions, sign language, posture, movement, and behavior.
misconceptions: It is not limited to hand gestures; gestures can originate from any bodily motion or state.
It is not the same as sign language recognition alone, which is only one area of the field.
It does not require physical contact with the device being controlled.
